title: What programming does: from an idea to a result
goal: Explain why we need a program, distinguish its text from its result and change one message yourself. No previous coding knowledge is required.

prerequisites.text: You only need to type and press a button. No mathematics, variables, compiler installation or programming experience is required.

sections.title: A computer needs a precise action
paragraphs: Imagine a display at a workshop entrance. While it is blank, visitors cannot tell whether the workshop is open. We want a clear greeting on the screen. A person can guess what we mean; a computer follows specified actions without knowing our intentions. First decide what a visitor should see, then choose how to express the instructions.

Programming means creating and checking programs to solve problems. A program specifies actions in a form a computing system can process. Our first action is simply to display a message. Other programs read data, calculate routes or control images. Writing text alone does not guarantee the intended result.

sections.title: Why C++ came about
paragraphs: Bjarne Stroustrup created C++. In 1979 at Bell Labs he began work on C with Classes, its predecessor. He wanted programs that could organise related parts while executing efficiently. C was an important foundation; Simula also influenced the use of classes. You do not need to learn C or understand classes before starting here: classes come later.

Why does this matter to you? Think of a game with many objects and repeated calculations. Its code must remain manageable and update the display in time. That illustrates the combination of concerns behind the language; it does not mean C++ is always faster than every other language. It is used for systems components, games and other resource-sensitive applications. A website, report or automation may use a different language according to its requirements and environment.

tables.caption: A few milestones, not dates to memorise
rows: Work on C with Classes began.
The first ISO C++ standard was published.

sections.title: Decide the result first
paragraphs: Our display has a simple agreement: after running, show Hello, Nexus! on its own line. That is the expected output. “Expected” matters: the lesson author supplied it as a reference. Actual output appears only after you run your own program in Practice. Comparing the two helps reveal mistakes.

Source code is the program text in a chosen language. A compiler checks that text and translates it into an executable form. Nexus builds C++ for the browser WebAssembly environment. Running executes the prepared program; output is just one possible result. Saving text, building a program and running it are different actions.

diagram.caption: From an idea to a check
diagram.text:
Task → source code → compilation → execution → actual output
                               ↑ error: correct the text
Expected output ↔ compare with actual output

sections.title: Read what the program should say
paragraphs: Below, source code and expected output are shown together. Look inside the double quotes. A person will see Hello, Nexus!; the quotes delimit the text in the language and are not printed. The \n sequence inside the string means a new line. It should not appear as two printed characters.

Do not try to reproduce the whole framework from memory. We change only the message for now. You still need to know what the surrounding lines do: the iostream header declares input/output facilities; main marks entry to our ordinary program; braces enclose its actions. This task does not require redesigning functions or libraries.

sections.title: Each symbol has a job
paragraphs: In std::cout << "Hello, Nexus!\n";, std::cout names the standard output stream and << sends the next item to it. std is the standard namespace; :: qualifies cout as belonging there. For our display it is a ready-made way to show text. Here << performs output; the same symbol can have another meaning elsewhere.

A semicolon ends this statement. int main() declares the main function: int describes its status result, and the parentheses here belong to a declaration with no parameters. return 0; finishes main successfully. That zero is not printed. #include <iostream> tells the preprocessor to include a header; it does not display text and has no semicolon. A library provides reusable facilities; a header describes access to relevant facilities. The two are related but different.

sections.title: Change exactly one thing
paragraphs: Before pressing Run my work, replace Nexus inside the quotes with workshop. Predict aloud: Hello, workshop! will appear. Then run. If you still see the old text, check that you edited your own workspace rather than merely viewed the example, and that the new run has finished.

In your own copy, try removing the closing quote. The compiler will reject the text, so the new program will not run. Restore the quote or use Undo, then run again. This is a useful observation: it identifies the stage that needs attention. The independent task below asks for a different greeting so you can apply the action rather than memorise a single line.

practice.title: On your own: greet a visitor
practice.task: The workshop display must show exactly one line: Welcome to the workshop! Change only the message in your starter, keeping the quotes and newline. Run it and explain why neither quotes nor zero appear in the output.
practice.stdinNote: Leave the input field empty: this task sets every value in the program.
criteria: Text and case match the task.
Output contains no quotes, literal \n or status 0.
You can identify the stage that detects a missing quote.
practice.hint: Find std::cout. Change the text between double quotes and keep \n before the closing quote.

passport.start: Your starter says Hello, Nexus!; the example is separate.
passport.where: Nexus → Practice → My independent work, main.cpp.
passport.knowledge: Quotes, output, newline, compilation and execution were introduced above.
passport.change: Only the text inside quotes; keep the framework.
passport.checks: Run without error and compare the line beside the button; explain separately.
passport.errors: Missing quote or semicolon; editing the example instead of your workspace.
passport.recovery: Undo your last change. You can view the starter without replacing your work.

exercises.task: First predict the output after replacing Nexus with workshop.

selfcheck.prompt: The code is saved. How can you know it displayed the intended message?
options: Run it and compare actual with expected output
selfcheck.feedback: Saving keeps text. Running produces an actual result; comparison checks it.

selfcheck.prompt: Removing a quote caused a compilation error. Did the new source run?
options: Yes, because the button was pressed
No: fix the text and build again
selfcheck.feedback: Pressing Run does not turn invalid source into a runnable program.
